extracted.intended_audience: comedians, humor scholars, students, and the general public interested in comedy ethics and controversial humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative dimensions for judging or producing controversial/edgy stand-up material (especially jokes about rape or other serious harms), balancing free-speech/artistic concerns with audience accountability and ethical impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free speech / artistic integrity claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Supporters of edgy comedians often appeal to ideals of free speech as integral to an artist’s integrity (e.g., 'If Tosh, or any comedian for that matter, has to watch what they say for fear of offending then we are in effect silencing their right to free expression of ideas').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recurrent defense of controversial material; the page stresses that invoking free speech does not automatically settle questions of taste, ethics, or social consequences — free expression does not immunize a performer from criticism or professional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability to audiences in the Internet age
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of increased access to audiences via the Internet, performers have increased responsibility to be accountable for things said to those audiences ('The benefit of increased access to audiences carries with it the increased responsibility to be accountable for things said to those audiences').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use past controversies (Michael Richards, Carlos Mencia, Tracy Morgan, Daniel Tosh) as evidence that digital amplification increases consequences; evaluate how public reaction and online circulation affect a comedian's career and public evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all rape jokes are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: Some rape jokes perpetuate a culture that is cool with rape and some don’t ('all rape jokes are not created equal, some perpetuate a culture that is cool with rape and some don’t').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the joke’s premise and effect: does it normalize, trivialize, or endorse sexual violence, or does it critique, satirize, or subvert harmful attitudes? Look beyond surface offensiveness to underlying social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid targeting a specific individual with rape-as-punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes that imagine or suggest rape of a named or present individual (e.g., 'wouldn’t it be funny if that girl got raped by like, 5 guys right now?') are described as not funny and not acceptable ('Because “wouldn’t it be funny if this woman got gang raped right now” isn’t a funny joke, it isn’t even a joke').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat hypotheticals that single out an audience member or identifiable person as especially harmful; consider safety and self-advocacy concerns of people in comedy spaces when judging such material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider who is 'allowed' to say what to whom (identity/power dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate jokes with attention to who is making them and who is their target — issues of who is 'allowed' to say what to whom matter in assessing appropriateness and harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in speaker identity, audience composition, and power imbalances; a joke that punches down at marginalized groups warrants different scrutiny than one that 'punches up.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy and potential to perpetuate harmful stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should be mindful of underlying premises that attack those already in marginalized positions; 'Perpetuating harmful stereotypes or world views should not be the purpose of comedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge material on whether it reinforces oppressive narratives. If a joke's effect is to demean or dehumanize a group, it fails on empathy grounds regardless of comic intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine performer’s broader body of work for patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: A comedian’s other material and public persona provide context for interpreting a problematic joke ('I’m actually still less troubled by Daniel Tosh’s joking about a heckler getting raped than I am by segments from his TV show...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use patterns in a performer's history (recurring themes or attitudes toward certain groups) to assess whether an instance is an isolated misstep or part of a broader harmful stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish legal/free-speech rights from moral/taste evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that having a legal right to say something does not preclude others from judging it tasteless, irresponsible, or despicable ('Tosh has the right to say whatever he wants... yet, that does not mean he’s inoculated from criticism').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always separate constitutional or legal permissibility from ethical, aesthetic, or professional evaluations when assessing comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience feedback and craft refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience responses (booing, heckling) are legitimate feedback mechanisms for performers to refine material; 'Finessing one’s material could entail a lifetime of studying, perfecting one’s craft/“art.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a comedian adapts and revises material in response to feedback or doubles down on harmful bits; professionalism includes learning from audience reactions rather than dismissing them as censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual suitability and attendee preparedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members also bear some responsibility to know what they are attending ('Perhaps they should have researched who was performing, BEFORE going to see if it was appropriate for them').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating incidents, weigh venue, advertised content, and reasonable expectations of attendees alongside performer behavior; however, this does not absolve performers of responsibility for targeted or especially harmful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false dichotomies; balance multiple evaluative axes
rubrics_metrics.description: The debate should not be reduced to binaries ('It is not my aim here to... whether such jokes are or are not appropriate... If these positions seem roughly sketched or resting upon a false dichotomy, that is because they are').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess jokes across several dimensions (artistic intent, craft, harm, context, audience, performer history) rather than forcing an either/or choice between 'free speech' and 'censorship.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is the punchline: victim vs. perpetrator / punch up vs punch down
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the joke makes the victim the butt of the joke or targets perpetrators/power structures (implicit in discussion of statistical sampling of rape jokes and who they target).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer constructions that 'punch up' (criticize power/abusers) rather than 'punch down' (mock victims); sampling or analysis of where the punchline lands can reveal whether a genre of jokes tends to reinforce harm.
